newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil soybean growers slow sales as prices ease.
newsitem.headline: Brazil soybean growers slow sales as prices ease.

text.p: With Brazil's 1996/97 soybean crop fully harvested, the rhythm of export sales has slowed as farmers hold on to the product in hopes of higher prices, agronomists said.
"Everything's been harvested -- now is more the moment for waiting," said Eloi Hilgert, economist at the research department of the Rio Grande do Sul agricultural secretariat.

Following the peak of the harvest in March and April, producers were sitting out a drop in international prices and will only be selling in dribs and drabs until mid-August when demand from domestic industries is likely to pick up.

"There are many people waiting for better prices, even though prices are already high," said Hilgert. "But they will have to sell because they have to plan the next stage, the planting of the 1997/98 crop."
At Paranagua, the main grain loading port, loading of soybeans had tapered off in favour of soymeal.

On June 12, there were four vessels loading soymeal and one loading a mixed cargo of soybeans and meal. There were seven vessels waiting to load soymeal, one waiting for soybeans and two for mixed cargoes.
The port loaded a record 2.78 million tonnes soybeans in the year to June 11, well above 1.30 million during the same period last year.

Soymeal loading dropped to 2.55 million tonnes in the year to date from 3.17 million at the same time in 1996, mainly due to a change in Brazil's export tax structure which made it more profitable to sell beans this year than soyproducts.
Santos also had a record year, loading 1.20 million tonnes of soybeans by the end of May, double the amount in 1996.
Around 80 percent of this year's expected crop has already been sold, above average for this period, said Flavio Franca, analyst at independent consultants Safras e Mercado.
"Probably from now on, growers will sell very slowly -- they're in no hurry because they have sold a lot and sold well," Franca said.
However, prices may not rise by as much as expected in the second semester, when stocks are lowest.

"This year market conditons are different because there is a big differential between old crop and new crop contracts in Chicago," he said. "This natural price increase in between harvests will be limited."
At worst, prices will remain the same as they are now. At best, any problems with the U.S. harvest will fuel a rise in Chicago prices which will be reflected in Brazil, Franca said.
"It's a pretty comfortable situation -- it gives farmers room to speculate on a problem with the U.S. harvest," he said.
Following this year's exceptionally profitable harvest, agronomists are already looking to prospects for next year.

Rio Grande do Sul, which saw drought cut its harvest to 4.6 million tonnes instead of initial expectations for 6.0 million tonnes, forecasts a 10- to 15-percent increase in planted area for next year and a harvest of 6.12 million tonnes.
Parana, the largest producing state, estimates it harvested 6.5 million tonnes this year but does not yet have a forecast for 1997/98.
